recommended_title: How Many Comparisons Change the Leader? Refit-Verified Influence Perturbations of Bradley-Terry Leaderboards Across Evaluation Designs
central_question: How small a verified perturbation of the underlying comparison data (dropping or flipping individual comparisons) suffices to change the top-1 or top-k of a ridge Bradley-Terry leaderboard, and how does this size differ across crowdsourced-vote, expert-human, LLM-judge, and sports evaluation designs?
central_thesis: An influence-ordered search that verifies each candidate with an exact refit finds rank-changing perturbations of tens of comparisons in every evaluated design. That is 62 of 135,622 crowdsourced Arena votes (0.046%), 92 of 3,355 expert MT-Bench judgments (2.7%), 143 of 2,400 GPT-4-judge judgments (6.0%) and 7 or 16 of roughly 1,300 NBA games per season, and the sets are about 16x smaller than random perturbations. Which design looks most fragile depends on whether size is counted in comparisons or as a fraction of the data, and on the target (top-1 versus top-k set). These sizes are verified upper bounds and descriptive, not causal, design effects.
narrative_rationale: The sealed final evaluation is complete and qualified: every integrity check passed, including replay determinism, zero failed episodes, the synthetic planted-minimum control and the row-permutation control. It reports verified perturbation sizes for 15 real cases (4 evaluation designs x {drop top-1, flip top-1, drop top-k}, with NBA split into two seasons) plus two controls, all identical across 3 seeds. That is a complete, reproducible cross-design measurement, which is exactly the open question the task poses. The evaluated finder is the AMIP-ordered prefix search itself (study.selection_kind = baseline; the program is identical to the baseline). The pre-declared superiority test against AMIP is therefore not supported (final.metric.claim_supported = 0; mean log2 ratio vs AMIP = 0 with CI [0, 0]), and a methods-superiority paper is impossible. Refined search variants were designed but never scored: all 3 attempts are unscored, which is missing evidence and not a measured loss. The strongest honest story is a measurement and methodology paper. It treats a refit-verified influence search as an instrument, validates that instrument with controls and the random and heuristic comparators, and uses it to answer the cross-design sensitivity question, including the finding that the answer depends on how perturbation size is scaled. This uses all the grounded evidence and claims no improvement.

The downstream study selected the baseline (selection_kind=baseline, search_score_delta=0.0) with 0 of 3 attempts scored. The paper therefore studies the baseline influence-ordered finder as its instrument and does not present any refined variant as a contribution.

The final evaluation outcome is 'qualified' with claim_supported=0. The paper reports the qualified evaluation as validating the measurement instrument, and states plainly that no superiority over the AMIP ordering is claimed or supported.

method_groups.name: Refit-verified influence-ordered perturbation search (AMIP-style one-step influence ranking + exponential/binary prefix search with exact ridge Bradley-Terry refits)
method_groups.include_reason: This is the measurement instrument that produced every verified size. It is presented as an adaptation of the approximate-maximum-influence-perturbation idea to leaderboard targets (top-1 margin, top-k set boundary), with drop and flip perturbations. It is not presented as a new algorithm that beats AMIP; the run shows it is the AMIP ordering itself.

method_groups.name: Random perturbation comparator (20 random draws per size; a size counts when a majority of draws change the target)
method_groups.include_reason: This is the noise-like reference that separates targeted fragility from generic sampling fragility. Grounded: mean clipped log2(k_random/k) = 3.975, 95% case-bootstrap CI [3.934, 4.0].

method_groups.name: Direct leader-challenger heuristic comparator (remove the leader's wins over the challenger first, then the leader's wins over the strongest other opponents)
method_groups.include_reason: A domain-intuitive deterministic attack that checks whether influence ordering adds anything over the obvious strategy. Grounded only at family level: the influence ordering matched or beat it in every case of the Arena, MT-Bench GPT-4 and NBA families (family scores 0.0). On MT-Bench human the heuristic was marginally smaller in at least one case (family log2 score -0.0053).

method_groups.name: Instrument validity controls (synthetic 3-player planted case with a brute-force exact minimum; row-permutation control on Arena; seed replay determinism)
method_groups.include_reason: These controls show the measured sizes are not artifacts of row order or nondeterminism, and that the search reaches the exact minimum where one is computable (synthetic and permutation control scores 0.0; replay match 1.0; failed episode fraction 0.0).

results_focus: Primary: verified perturbation size for each of 5 data sources (Arena-140k, MT-Bench human, MT-Bench GPT-4 judge, NBA 2014, NBA 2015) x 3 targets (drop top-1, flip top-1, drop top-k), shown both as an absolute count and as a fraction of comparisons. Grounded in final.evidence.episodes verified_k and the final.metric.*_top1_{drop,flip}_frac values.

Scale dependence of cross-design conclusions. As a fraction, the crowdsourced Arena leader is the most fragile (0.046% drop) and the GPT-4-judge leader the least (6.0%). As an absolute count, NBA is the most fragile (7 and 16 games), and Arena (62) needs fewer comparisons than both MT-Bench designs (92 and 143) yet more than NBA. Present this as the paper's main conceptual point about how to compare designs.

Target dependence: top-k set changes can be much cheaper than top-1 changes (NBA top-5: 1 game in both seasons; Arena top-5: 21 vs 62 for top-1). On MT-Bench they cost more (top-3 drop: human 229, GPT-4 150). Flipping consistently needs fewer rows than dropping (Arena 46 vs 62, MT-Bench human 46 vs 92, GPT-4 61 vs 143, NBA 4 vs 7 and 8 vs 16).

Same questions, different judges: on MT-Bench the GPT-4-judge leader needs more drops than the human-expert leader for top-1 (143 vs 92, flip 61 vs 46), but the ordering reverses for the top-3 set (150 vs 229). The judge effect is therefore target-dependent, and the datasets also differ in size (2,400 vs 3,355).

Instrument validity: mean clipped log2 ratio vs random 3.975 [3.934, 4.0] (about 16x smaller, censored at the clip of 4); mean log2 ratio vs AMIP 0 [0, 0] (the instrument is the AMIP ordering); synthetic exact minimum recovered; permutation-invariant; deterministic across seeds 101-103; each seed's full 17-case suite ran in about 16 CPU seconds.
Explicit negative and qualification result: the pre-declared test of superiority over the AMIP ordering is not supported, and no refined search variant was evaluated.
figure_plan: Figure 1 (overview, page 1-2, full text width): a protocol schematic. Four evaluation designs feed comparison rows into a ridge Bradley-Terry fit, which gives a leaderboard with a leader/challenger (or top-k boundary). One-step influence scores order the rows; prefix search verifies each candidate with an exact refit, yielding a verified size k and the size measures (count and fraction). The random and heuristic comparators and the synthetic and permutation controls sit alongside.

Figure 2 (main result, full text width, 2 panels): grouped dot or bar plot of verified size per data source (5 categories) x target (3 series: drop top-1, flip top-1, drop top-k). Panel (a) shows the absolute count on a log axis; panel (b) shows the fraction of comparisons on a log axis. The visual contrast between the panels carries the scale-dependence point.

Figure 3 (controlled comparisons, full text width, 2 panels): (a) a dumbbell plot of MT-Bench human vs GPT-4 judge across the 3 targets (fraction of comparisons); (b) a slope chart of the design ordering for drop top-1 under count vs fraction, with 4 design families (NBA as two seasons or a season mean, labelled).

Table 1: evaluation designs and cases (source, design type, comparisons n, ties handling, top-k used, snapshot). Table 2: instrument validation and comparator summary. Appendix Table: all 17 per-case verified sizes per seed.

figure_specs.purpose: Give immediate glance value: what is perturbed (comparison rows), what estimator and target are tested, how the influence-ordered search is verified by exact refits, and which comparators and controls calibrate the instrument across the four evaluation designs.
figure_specs.layout_rationale: The ICLR 2026 template is single-column with a 5.5 in text width (paper.sty \textwidth 5.5in), so every figure spans the text block. A left-to-right flow with roughly 5 stages and a side band for comparators and controls fits a wide, short aspect ratio (about 3:1) and stays legible at 8-9 pt label size. Place it at the top of page 2 or the bottom of page 1.

figure_specs.purpose: Show the main result: the verified perturbation size for each data source and target, on an absolute-count scale and a fraction-of-data scale, so the reader sees that the cross-design ordering depends on the scale.
figure_specs.group_by: data_source (Arena-140k, MT-Bench human, MT-Bench GPT-4, NBA 2014, NBA 2015)
figure_specs.metric: verified perturbation size k (panel a, log10 axis) and k/n (panel b, log10 axis, percent)
figure_specs.split_by: target (drop top-1, flip top-1, drop top-k with k=5 for Arena/NBA and k=3 for MT-Bench)
figure_specs.layout_rationale: Two side-by-side panels with 5 categories and 3 series each need about 2.6 in per panel to keep tick labels horizontal or at 30 degrees at 8 pt. That only fits across the full 5.5 in single-column text width. Annotate the bar or dot values with the integer k (panel a) to avoid a separate table in the main body. Use the same colour per target in both panels.

figure_specs.purpose: Isolate two comparisons: (a) same MT-Bench questions judged by human experts vs GPT-4, across targets; (b) how the design ordering for drop top-1 flips between count and fraction scales.
figure_specs.group_by: panel a: target; panel b: design family
figure_specs.metric: panel a: k/n (%) for human and GPT-4 judge; panel b: rank (or log value) of drop top-1 size under count and under fraction
figure_specs.layout_rationale: Two compact panels (3 rows of dumbbells; a slope chart with 4-5 lines) sit side by side across the single-column text width at about 2.4 in tall. Column-width is the text width in this template, so the full-width span is required. Direct labels on line ends replace legends in panel b.

supplementary_plan.purpose: Give the full per-case and per-seed evidence, the exact estimator, evaluator and comparator definitions needed for reimplementation, the derivation of case sizes, the reproducibility record, the LLM-usage statement required by ICLR, and an honest account of the refined search variants that were designed but never evaluated. None of this material is essential to the central thesis, which is fully supported in the main body.

planned_subsections.heading: Per-case verified perturbation sizes for all seeds
planned_subsections.grounded_content: Table of all 17 cases (15 real + synthetic + permutation) x seeds 101/102/103 verified sizes, showing they are identical across seeds, plus per-seed run durations (about 15.5-16.3 s).

planned_subsections.heading: Estimator, targets and case construction
planned_subsections.grounded_content: Ridge Bradley-Terry MLE (ridge 0.1, ties as half wins, float64, damped Newton), a change counted only above tol 1e-6, removal of players with fewer than 50 comparisons, top-1 and top-k set definitions, which rows can be flipped (ties cannot), per-case row and player relabelling. Case sizes n derived as verified k divided by the reported fraction: Arena 135,622; MT-Bench human 3,355; MT-Bench GPT-4 2,400; NBA 2014 1,319; NBA 2015 1,311.

planned_subsections.heading: Comparators, controls and summary statistics
planned_subsections.grounded_content: Definitions of the random comparator (20 draws, majority rule, search capped at half the rows), the direct-pair heuristic, the clipped log2 ratio (clip at +/-4) and the case-level bootstrap (2,000 replicates). Synthetic planted control (3 players, brute-force exact minimum, score 0 so the minimum was recovered) and row-permutation control (score 0, identical size). Family-level comparator scores, including the MT-Bench human value of -0.0053.

planned_subsections.heading: Pre-declared superiority test and unevaluated refinements
planned_subsections.grounded_content: States that the pre-declared claim of improvement over the AMIP ordering (case-bootstrap CI lower bound of the log2 ratio > 0) is not supported (claim_supported = 0; mean 0, CI [0, 0]) because the evaluated instrument is that ordering. Records that 3 refined search configurations (category-count relinearized search with pruning and swap refinement) were designed, but 0 of 3 were scored because of execution-infrastructure failures. Their effect is unknown, not negative. The final evaluation's qualification status is completed and qualified.

planned_subsections.heading: Reproducibility record and LLM usage
planned_subsections.grounded_content: Data sources with pinned commits and checksums from the task data manifest; the numpy 2.2.6 / scipy 1.15.3 environment; seeds 101-103; CPU-only budget (4 cores, 8 GB); run commands; the mapping from each figure and table to the script that generates it. A separate LLM Usage section disclosing LLM assistance in ideation, implementation and writing.

notes_for_writer: Organize thesis-first. Sections: Introduction (question, thesis, 3-4 verifiable contributions); Related Work (drop-data robustness/AMIP and influence functions; pairwise-comparison ranking models; leaderboard manipulation and evaluation practice; LLM-as-judge); Problem Setup (estimator, targets, perturbations, two size scales and why both); Method (influence ordering for drop and flip, exact-refit prefix verification, why sizes are upper bounds, comparators, controls); Experimental Setup (designs/cases table); Results (instrument validity -> main cross-design result -> drop vs flip and top-1 vs top-k -> controlled contrasts: judge and scale); Discussion and Limitations; Conclusion. Appendix: LLM Usage, reproducibility, per-case tables, definitions, pre-declared test and unevaluated refinements.

Qualification disclosure: say the sealed final evaluation completed with all integrity checks passing (final.qualification.outcome = qualified, status = completed). Keep this separate from the pre-declared superiority test, which is NOT supported (final.metric.claim_supported = 0; mean log2 ratio vs AMIP 0.0, CI [0.0, 0.0]). Explain that this is by construction: the evaluated instrument is the AMIP-ordered search, identical to the baseline configuration. Never write that any configuration improved on AMIP.

Search vs final: the selection used search evidence only (study.selection_kind = baseline, study.search_score_delta = 0.0, study.investigation_outcome = completed_no_winner). All headline numbers come from the sealed final evaluation (final.*). Do not mix search-plane datasets (Arena-55k, NBA 1983-84) into the results; at most, mention in the appendix that a separate development split was used for selection.

Unscored attempts: 3 of 3 refined-variant attempts were unscored (study.attempts.unscored = 3). Describe them as not evaluated because of execution failures, with unknown effect. Never call them worse, failed methods, or refuted. Keep them out of the method section's main line.

Every size is an upper bound on the true minimal perturbation (a verified sufficient set), not a certified minimum. The only exact-minimum check is the synthetic 3-player control, where the search matched the brute-force minimum. Phrase results as 'a verified set of k comparisons suffices to ...'.

Uncertainty: the three seeds give identical sizes because the instrument is deterministic (replay match 1.0). Present this as determinism, not as variance across runs. The only interval in the artifacts is the case-level bootstrap CI for the log2 ratio vs random [3.934, 4.0]; note it is computed on log2 ratios clipped at 4, so 'about 16x' is a censored lower summary. There is NO sampling uncertainty over data resamples (e.g. bootstrap CIs on k); list this as a limitation, not as done.

Case sizes n: derive them exactly as verified k / reported fraction (Arena 135,622; MT-Bench human 3,355; GPT-4 2,400; NBA 2014 1,319; NBA 2015 1,311) and state the derivation in the appendix. Compute non-top-1 fractions (e.g. Arena top-5 21/135,622 = 0.015%, MT-Bench human top-3 229/3,355 = 6.8%, GPT-4 top-3 150/2,400 = 6.25%, NBA top-5 1/1,319 and 1/1,311 ~ 0.08%) from these and label them as derived. Do not report participant counts unless a reproducible script computes them after the 50-comparison filter; do not guess them.

Cross-design comparisons are descriptive. Differences are confounded with data size, number of participants, comparison-graph structure, tie rate and the leader's margin. Do not attribute differences causally to 'crowd vs expert vs judge vs sport'. The MT-Bench human vs GPT-4 contrast is the closest controlled comparison (same benchmark questions), but n still differs (3,355 vs 2,400), and the direction reverses between top-1 and top-3.

The heuristic comparator is grounded only at the family level. Say the influence ordering matched or beat it in all Arena, GPT-4-judge and NBA cases, and that on MT-Bench human the direct heuristic found a marginally smaller set in at least one case (family log2 score -0.0053). Do not invent per-case heuristic sizes.
Random comparator: report the mean clipped log2 ratio 3.975 (CI 3.934-4.0), roughly 16x. Do not report per-case random sizes; they are not in the grounded artifacts.
Use the reported NBA family fractions (0.876% drop, 0.457% flip) as the season mean, and per-season k (7/16 drop, 4/8 flip, 1/1 top-5) from the verified sizes.

Citations: references.bib is mostly off-topic retrieval noise. Cite only relevant entries: Broderick2020AnAF (AMIP / drop-data robustness), Giordano2019AHS (infinitesimal jackknife), Monari2000WithdrawingAE (analytic effect of withdrawing an example), and optionally Alaa2020DiscriminativeJQ (higher-order influence). Do NOT cite the unrelated entries (radiotherapy, Duffing oscillators, teak biomass, etc.). The starter literature named in the task brief (Bradley-Terry 1952; Chatbot Arena; MT-Bench/LLM-as-a-judge; influence functions (Koh & Liang); vote rigging; Leaderboard Illusion) is essential context. Add it to the bib only through the pipeline's grounded reference mechanism. If it cannot be added, describe the ideas without fabricated keys. Describe these works only at the level of the brief's one-line descriptions. For the starter item on dropping preferences in LLM rankings, cite it as prior work on Arena-style rankings without claiming knowledge of its results, and position this paper's contribution as the cross-design, drop-vs-flip, top-1-vs-top-k and scale-dependence analysis with validated controls, not as the first observation that Arena leaders are fragile.

Venue (ICLR 2026): double-blind, so no names or self-identifying links; the body must fill 8-9 pages with page 8 at least 75% full. Use the space for a precise problem setup, a method section explaining mechanistically why first-order influence on the leader-challenger margin should rank rows well (rows with large residuals on edges adjacent to the leader or challenger dominate), and a substantive limitations section. Do not pad. Include an 'LLM Usage' section (appendix allowed). ICLR has no mandatory checklist; add a short Reproducibility Statement.

Figures: export every quantitative plot as PDF (referenced from LaTeX) plus a 300-DPI PNG. Raster-only output must be at least 2400 px wide since all figures are full-width. Use one consistent colour per target (drop top-1, flip top-1, drop top-k) across figures, and one per design family. The overview figure uses generate-concept-figure; it is the only concept figure.

Reader-facing labels: 'verified perturbation size', 'fraction of comparisons', 'leader change (top-1)', 'top-k set change', 'crowdsourced votes / expert human / LLM judge / sports'. Use 'configuration' and 'seeded run' instead of internal pipeline terms.
